title: Your old men shall dream (Joel 2:28–29)
hook: I will pour out my spirit on all flesh; Peter quoted it at Pentecost

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hosea's parent on their knees: I taught Ephraim to walk. Your line was cords of love. Did you guide someone small without needing the credit? Day four hundred eighty-three.

Nine in the morning in Jerusalem, a festival crowd in the streets, and a commotion. A small group of Jesus's followers are pouring out of a house, talking in languages they never learned, and visitors from all over the Mediterranean hear their own home tongues. Some people are amazed. Others laugh: they're drunk. Then Peter, a fisherman who weeks earlier had denied he even knew Jesus, stands up. He says, more or less, it's too early in the day for that. And instead of explaining it himself, he reaches back hundreds of years and quotes an old prophet, a short book most people today couldn't find in their Bibles. The prophet is Joel.
screen: `NINE IN THE MORNING, A FESTIVAL CROWD.`

segments.voice: Joel is only three or four chapters long, and nobody is sure exactly when he lived. His book opens with a disaster: a plague of locusts that strips the land bare. He calls the people to fast and to turn back to God, and then the promises come, first of rain and harvest, and then something bigger. In the King James Bible: "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions." Look at who is on that list. Sons and daughters, not just sons. Old and young. And the next verse goes further: "And also upon the servants and upon the handmaids in those days will I pour out my spirit." Servants. In the ancient world, the spirit of God was usually something that came on a chosen few: a prophet, a judge, a king. Joel pictures it soaked into everyone, the way rain soaks a field after the locusts. Old people dreaming is not a small detail either. It means nobody has aged out of hearing from God. Then the scene in Acts chapter two. Peter tells the crowd, in the King James wording: "But this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel." Christians remember that day as Pentecost, and many call it the birthday of the church. Jews read Joel too, and hear his promise in their own way, as a hope for Israel's renewal. For Christians, Peter's sermon made Joel's list the guest list of the church. And look back at this week: a field bought in wartime, dry bones, a heart of flesh, a furnace, a lions' den, a parent teaching a child to walk, and now the spirit on everyone. Over and over, the prophets refuse to give up on people.
screen: then, large: `YOUR OLD MEN SHALL DREAM DREAMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to someone old and someone young. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the oldest person you know and the youngest person you know. Picture each of their faces. Ask yourself: when did I last really listen to either of them, without fixing or correcting? What might the old one still be dreaming? What might the young one be seeing that you've stopped seeing? Just hold them both for a moment. If you pray, you can pray Joel's promise over them in its own words. If you don't, simply decide which one you'll call or sit with this week. The bell holds the time.
Your old men shall dream. Joel's promise that the spirit of God would pour out on everyone, young and old, women and men, servants too.
screen: `YOUR OLD MEN SHALL DREAM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: on all flesh. Today, ask one older person what they still hope for, and one younger person what they see coming. Then just listen. Day four hundred eighty-three, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: Christians read Joel 2:28–29 every year around Pentecost, alongside Acts 2, where Peter quotes it; many churches celebrate Pentecost seven weeks after Easter as the coming of the Holy Spirit.

fork.setup: you're Peter. a crowd hears your friends speaking in other languages, and some laugh that you're all drunk. what do you do?
options: slip away before it gets worse.
stand up and quote an old prophet.
argue about how much wine is too much.
fork.reveal: he stands up, says it's far too early in the day to be drunk, and quotes Joel: "this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel."

original.note: Hebrew: spirit, breath, wind. what Joel says God will pour out on all flesh.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about grandparents having nice dreams.
what it means: Joel pictures God's spirit poured on everyone, not just a chosen few: daughters, the old, even servants.
what a scholar hears: in Hebrew Bibles these verses are numbered Joel 3:1–2, and Acts 2:17–18 quotes them, changing afterward to in the last days.

notes: Joel is three chapters in English Bibles and four in Hebrew Bibles (where 2:28–32 becomes chapter 3); hence 'three or four chapters'. Confirm.
Joel's date is genuinely disputed (proposals range from the 9th to the 4th century BC); stated as unknown.
Acts 2:15 'the third hour of the day' rendered as nine in the morning. Confirm.
Acts 2:17 'in the last days' replaces Joel's 'afterward'; stated in the trapdoor. Confirm.
Jewish reading of Joel described briefly and without ranking ('a hope for Israel's renewal'). A Keeper may wish to adjust.
'Many call it the birthday of the church' is a common Christian description; not universal.
